item.title: Wisconsin family to keep logging 1,800 acres as $1.6 million deal blocks development
item.description: A Wisconsin family will continue to own and manage nearly 1,800 acres of forest under a proposed $1.6 million conservation easement. The deal would block development, keep timber production going and open almost 1,500 acres to hiking, hunting and fishing, while also protecting part of the Ice Age National Scenic Trail.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Two young scientists bought 116 acres in 1997; 25 years later, they protected it for wildlife
item.description: In 1997, young scientists Laura Bonk and Phil Trowbridge bought 116 acres beside New Hampshire’s Bear Brook State Park. About 25 years later, they placed the entire Derevya Farms property under a permanent conservation easement while retaining ownership, protecting its forests, wetlands, waterways and wildlife habitat.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: How a $25,000 beach cottage in Cape Cod became one of the most iconic homes in American history
item.description: Nestled in Cape Cod, the Kennedy Compound holds significant historical weight for the Kennedy family. Acquired in 1928, it functioned as a gathering place for pivotal family moments and events. This summer retreat was especially relevant during President John F. Kennedy's administration, influencing their legacy. The compound witnessed both joyous occasions and sorrowful events, cementing its importance.

item.title: Camp Mystic owners seek to sell the Texas girls’ camp after 2025 flood; the bankruptcy plan puts its entire 749-acre riverfront property up for auction
item.description: Camp Mystic, a century-old Christian girls' camp in Texas, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy following catastrophic flooding in 2025 which killed 28 people. The camp's owners plan to auction off property and other assets to repay creditors. Victims' families oppose the sale, demanding accountability and transparency concerning the camp's operations. Investigations revealed negligence in the camp's response to a flash flood alert prior to the incident.

item.title: Floating solar cuts seabed light in French Polynesia, with no detectable lagoon temperature
item.description: Floating photovoltaic platforms in a French Polynesian lagoon created substantial reductions in light reaching the seabed, which was studied for one year. Researchers monitored the environmental impact of four platforms and a control area during the study. They observed strong attenuation in ultraviolet radiation under the platforms, affecting diverse wavelengths. However, changes in water temperature remained statistically insignificant and below sensor accuracy levels.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: 14-year-old Jia Mingxuan builds tree-saving device that wins gold in Germany
item.description: At 14, Jia Mingxuan turned a childhood view of Aohan’s dry landscape into a simple device designed to capture atmospheric moisture for young trees. Built from steel tubes and recycled plastic bottles, his prototype uses condensation to direct water towards sapling roots. The invention won gold at the 2025 Nuremberg International Invention Exhibition.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: 55-million-year-old fossil bird shows how trogons evolved their unusual feet
item.description: A fossil of Daniatrogon kochi, discovered in Denmark, provides insights into the evolution of trogon feet. Researchers found that the trogons' unique foot morphology developed gradually over time. The fossil also shows changes in the shape of their beaks, which were narrower than those of modern species. Additionally, early trogoniforms displayed more varied beak and foot shapes, indicating a diverse ecology.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Minnesota picks 57-acre Lakeville site for $1 billion horticulture Expo 2031
item.description: Minnesota has selected Lakeville as the planned host city for Expo 2031, a horticulture-focused international exhibition expected to attract millions of visitors. Organisers have secured a purchase agreement for 57 acres, while more land is expected to be assembled for the six-month event. Plans include pavilions, gardens, an amphitheatre and developments intended to remain after the Expo.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Ancient school where Aristotle taught Alexander the Great has been unearthed by archaeologists in Greece
item.description: In an extraordinary archaeological discovery in northern Greece, a gymnasium complex tied to Alexander the Great's education has emerged in Mieza. Believed to have been established by King Philip II, this site functioned as a prestigious institution for the elite. Recent excavations revealed various structures, including banquet halls used for social gatherings and teaching facilities, hinting at Aristotle's influence on students like Alexander.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Private Effort Protects Reservoir: Landowner’s project restores creek; safeguards Kinkaid Lake water
item.description: Greg Reising began his conservation work on his 100-acre property near Kinkaid Lake in 1995. He transformed former agricultural land by establishing prairie vegetation and planting thousands of trees. Erosion and sedimentation problems in the Kinkaid Lake watershed led to broader conservation efforts involving various agencies. The Environmental Quality Incentives Program supported Reising's initiatives, including streambank stabilization and habitat improvement measures.

item.title: ‘Took turns shooting’: Trans NYT exec killed by in-laws amid anti-LGBTQ+ allegations
item.description: Jonathan McKinsey was shot and killed by his elderly in-laws at a sports complex in California. Police arrested the suspects, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, near the crime scene shortly after the incident. McKinsey's transgender identity allegedly contributed to a family conflict and legal disputes with his wife, Candice Jang. The couple was involved in divorce proceedings and allegations of domestic violence prior to McKinsey's death.

item.title: US military to guard midterms after Trump gutted agency that protects elections
item.description: The National Security Agency and other military cyber units have long assisted with monitoring election infrastructure and defending it against possible hacking attempts. Election systems were designated as “critical infrastructure” in 2017, paving the way for greater federal cybersecurity support. Hegseth's announcement comes weeks before Election Day on November 3, with early voting already underway.
